a.raw: oh im so happy to be here she cried
a.why: Opening quotation mark, a capital on Oh with a comma after it, a capital I and an apostrophe in I’m, the exclamation point inside the closing quotation mark, and a period after the dialogue tag.

b.raw: oh im going to love it here anne whispered
b.why: Same pattern as the model: quotation marks around her words, Oh followed by a comma, a capital I and an apostrophe in I’m, the exclamation point inside the quotation marks. One thing more: Anne is a name, so it takes a capital even in the middle of the sentence.

match.placid: Placid is not a person or a happy feeling. Think of a pond with no ripples on it at all.
match.imagine: Imagine is something you do, so its meaning should start with “to.”
match.companion: Hidden inside companion is an old word for bread: the person who shares your bread. Look for a person.
match.delight: Delight is a feeling, and a big one. Look for the meaning about joy.

copia.seed: Matthew Cuthbert and the sorrel mare jogged comfortably over the eight miles to Bright River.

Matthew Cuthbert and the sorrel mare jogged comfortably over the eight miles to Bright River, past snug farmsteads and blossoming orchards.

connector: Yesterday Mrs. Rachel sat at her window and could not work out where Matthew was going. Today you ride along with him. He drives eight miles to collect a boy, and finds somebody else waiting for him, somebody who does not stop talking. Listen to her closely. By the end of the chapter you should be able to hear Anne with your eyes shut.

transcripts.welcome: Today's question is about voice. Everybody you know sounds like themselves — so what is it, exactly, that makes Anne sound like Anne and like nobody else? By the end of the lesson you will be able to point to what makes her voice hers. Keep yesterday's plurals close as well. You will meet them again in the word work, before you open the book.
transcripts.guide1: Same skill as yesterday. Narrator, and character. Chapter two has the same shape of title as chapter one — somebody else gets surprised. Watch who. First, though, words. You're still on the word parts that mean with, or together, and today they matter more than usual, because chapter two is about two people meeting who were not expecting each other at all.
transcripts.guide2: Matthew goes to the station expecting a boy and finds a girl who does not stop talking. Listen to what she does on the drive home. A road under the trees, a pond, a view — Anne will not let any of them stay ordinary. Ask yourself why a girl with nothing of her own would want to give everything a name. And keep an eye on quiet Matthew while she does it.
transcripts.guide3: Matthew went for a boy and came home with Anne, and said almost nothing the whole way. Now the questions. As you answer, think about how much you knew about Matthew even though he barely spoke. That is voice. And it is what you're building into your own character today — not a description. A way of being in the world.
transcripts.wgrd: Here is a trick worth keeping for the rest of the year. A narrator can stand beside a character and say nothing, and you end up seeing through that character's eyes without noticing. Today you ride with Matthew. When a plain road suddenly sounds beautiful, stop and ask whose idea that was. The narrator's, or Anne's? The answer tells you whose eyes you are borrowing.
transcripts.dol: Today's broken sentence is somebody talking, and people talking are the hardest thing to punctuate. Something is missing around the words she says. Something is missing inside a word that has been squeezed short. And a little word at the very front wants a pause after it. Look hard at the model first. Everything you need is sitting in it.
transcripts.morphology: You know these two word parts already. Both mean with, or together. Here is why they are worth the practice. Once you can spot them, a long word stops being a wall and becomes two pieces you can take apart. And today's hidden surprise is the one that means bread. A companion, long ago, was simply someone you shared your bread with.
transcripts.vocabulary: Yesterday you pulled these four words apart. Today you only have to remember them. That is the real test of a word: not whether you understood it once, but whether it comes back when you need it. Match them quickly if you can. If one hesitates, notice which one. That is the word to use in a sentence of your own today.
transcripts.grammar: Most words make a plural the easy way. You add a letter and move on. The ones in today's sentence refuse. They change their middle, or grow an old ending, or keep a shape from hundreds of years ago. That is why readers trip on them and writers get them wrong. Hunt all three down, and don't stop at the first.
transcripts.spelling: Here is the secret behind this week's spelling. You can usually hear the rule before you see it. Say a word out loud with more than one, and listen. If your mouth needs an extra beat at the end, or if a y at the end of the word has to change, that word is doing something more than the ordinary. Let your ear find them.
transcripts.read: One chapter today, and most of it happens in a buggy. Two people who have never met sit side by side for eight miles, and only one of them talks. As you read, keep a rough count in your head of how many things Anne gives a new name to. Then, when the chapter ends, ask yourself what a girl who names everything might be hoping for.
transcripts.chapter: These three questions look simple, and they are, on the surface. Underneath them is a harder one. Is Anne as happy as she sounds? She talks and talks, and she names everything she sees. But go back to the very first thing she says to Matthew at the station. When you describe her, don't stop at what she looks like. Think about what she was afraid of.
transcripts.wordconn: Your grammar answer is already saved, so this is just a moment to connect it. All week you have been looking at words that break the ordinary rule. They were supposed to behave one way, and they turned out another. Today's chapter does the same thing with a person. Matthew was expecting a boy. The rule said a boy. What was waiting at the station was Anne.
transcripts.workshop: Here is one move to try from today's chapter. Anne does not just see a road. She gives it a name that nobody else would have thought of. That is voice, working on a single word. Before you write your two or three sentences, decide one thing your character would call by a name of their own. Then let them say it out loud.
